A1.notes.Q3: Course performance is useful but must yield ~10 extra students to justify it over our current credit-based rule. High school GPA and nationality feel too predictive of social status rather than academic struggle. Disability data could be crucial if accurate; financial aid seems most ethically justifiable given existing vulnerability markers.
A1.notes.Q4: As an advisor, I need to know exactly *why* a student is flagged so they can explain it away or address the root cause. Without clear reasons, students will feel targeted and distrustful, leading them to hide problems rather than seek help.

A2.notes.Q3: Course grades are essential for me (Large threshold). Admissions data adds some context but isn't critical yet (Moderate). Tracking Absalon clicks feels like surveillance without direct impact on support; I'd prefer we just call them based on credit failure. Disability info must be huge to justify, likely only if it triggers a specific safety check rather than general help.
A2.notes.Q4: Trust is everything here. If I can't tell a student why they were flagged, the 'support' feels like punishment rather than help. High explainability is mandatory for any proactive contact; otherwise students will disengage.
A2.notes.Q5: We need to reach everyone who falls behind, not just a convenient majority. Missing vulnerable groups creates inequality that hurts the university's mission more than it helps efficiency.
A2.notes.Q6: One-off emails get lost in the inbox stream. If a model says there's an issue, it needs immediate attention from me as their advisor to ensure we actually offer help.
A2.notes.Q7: For generic emails, a small net gain in reach is worth the minor annoyance of unnecessary contact because we don't know who needs it otherwise. For personalized advice from me, false positives waste precious time and trust.

A3.notes.Q3: Course performance is useful, but Absalon data feels like surveillance without clear benefit for me as an advisor.
A3.notes.Q4: Students need to understand why they are flagged, or the email support will be ignored.
A3.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling student hurts more than unnecessary contact with others; equity is non-negotiable for me.
A3.notes.Q6: Early intervention is critical; waiting for formal dropout markers means losing the window of opportunity.
A3.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach carries risk but high value; I'd rather get it right than overwhelm students with noise.

S1.notes.Q3: Basic grades make sense, but age/gender are too invasive for prediction without huge benefit. Disability data is okay only if it truly helps me get help immediately.
S1.notes.Q4: As a former dropout, I need to know exactly WHY I was flagged so my advisor can help me fix the real issue, not just guess.
S1.notes.Q5: My friends in different nationalities are often unfairly ignored because 'average' data doesn't fit them. We can't afford to miss students like me who are already at a disadvantage.
S1.notes.Q6: Don't wait until the end of my studies to warn me. If I'm falling behind, I need support now in the café while working.
S1.Q8.1: If we flag me too many times, I might just ignore the emails and drop out completely instead of asking for help.

S2.notes.Q3: Grades help me track my own work, so that data is okay if it helps find struggling peers quickly (small threshold). Admissions data adds context on background but doesn't explain *why* I'm failing, making privacy trade-offs heavier (moderate/large for sensitive bits like financial aid which often overlap with struggle). Age and race are purely discriminatory proxies; unacceptable unless fairness gains are huge.
S2.notes.Q4: I need explanation because I might flag myself or friends if the logic isn't clear (e.g., 'low credits' vs 'mental health issue'). High explainability allows me to decide whether to reach out for my own help, which builds trust.
S2.notes.Q5: If Group B (women/immigrants) are under-identified, losing a few students to fix fairness feels right; we shouldn't help everyone equally if the 'everyone' excludes vulnerable groups entirely.
S2.notes.Q6: A personalized email feels more supportive and less intrusive than a cold 'generic' blast, but requires trust in that being confidential.
S2.notes.Q7: With generic emails, spamming creates noise and erodes trust. Contact too few students and we miss real help-needs; aim for middle ground.
S2.Q8.1: The biggest concern is algorithmic bias reinforcing existing social hierarchies without transparency about how decisions are made and who holds oversight power over them.

S3.notes.Q3: Course performance helps but grades are already known to me; I need more help, not just 'failed' flags. Disability data is too sensitive unless it's for my own support plan only.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to know EXACTLY why I'm being flagged so an advisor can help me specifically, not with a vague pattern match.
S3.notes.Q5: If the model misses me because it assumes healthy people study harder, that's worse than missing someone else slightly more often. I want to be found before I drop out.
S3.notes.Q6: Don't let my semester slow down cause me to disappear from the system. Continuous monitoring feels right for someone managing a chronic condition.
S3.Q8.1: I worry the system might use my disability data to limit which courses I can register for or lower my credit threshold unfairly.

S4.notes.Q3: I need clear warnings about ADHD deadlines, so high-school GPA helps context. But Absalon data feels like watching me study; too invasive unless the model finds a pattern I missed (small gain). Sensitive disability data is vital for fairness but scary to share without strict guarantees.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I'm flagged, like 'late submissions on complex modules'. A black box is okay if it's better at finding me early (large gain), but for support meetings, a clear reason builds trust more.
S4.notes.Q5: It hurts when the system misses my disability context because it flags other Danish students more easily than me. Missing people is worse than false alarms here; I'd accept a slight drop in total catches to ensure equity.
S4.notes.Q6: If the system flags me, I want immediate help regarding my ADHD and past dropout struggles. Waiting a year means losing momentum during critical exam periods.
S4.Q8.1: There should be a 'pause button' where any identified student can ask why they were picked up and demand no contact if they believe it's wrong or irrelevant to their actual needs.

S5.notes.Q3: I am new here and don't want to be profiled deeply on non-essential data like nationality or race, but missing a disability-specific help is dangerous.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged so I don't feel punished without cause.
S5.notes.Q5: As a first-gen international student, it hurts more if the system doesn't find me even when I am struggling due to my background.
S5.notes.Q6: If the system says something is wrong, I want help immediately, not just once a year.
S5.notes.Q7: A personalized email feels like harassment if I am not truly struggling; a general info email is less invasive but also safer.
S5.Q8.1: I worry that the threshold for flagging might be set too high because it's easier to prove academic failure than emotional distress or cultural adaptation issues, leading us to miss those really in need.

S6.notes.Q3: Using just grades/credits is okay if it helps a lot (moderate gain). High school data feels too invasive about my background since I moved countries online learning platform activity like page views feels creepy and unnecessary; only for big gains. Sensitive info makes me pause unless there's huge benefit.
S6.notes.Q4: I cannot accept a model that can't explain why I'm flagged, especially since my language barrier might skew results unfairly.
S6.notes.Q5: It's unfair if certain groups get overlooked more than others just because of bias in data or models that don't know about my specific situation as a second language speaker.
S6.notes.Q6: Proactive outreach is necessary; waiting until I fail courses leaves no time for intervention, which often leads to giving up.
S6.Q8.1: Teachers often grade Danish differently than EU law, making me look worse unfairly. Models need to account for that context.

S7.notes.Q3: Grades help me track my progress; I accept a threshold for that to find struggling peers. Admission data seems too broad compared to actual performance, and online activity (Absalon) feels like surveillance since it's already public but adds pressure.
S7.notes.Q4: I care deeply about transparency as it builds trust between advisor and student. Very low explainability is hard to accept without massive gains, but I'd prefer missing a few cases over having an opaque black box that might mistake me for struggling.
S7.notes.Q5: Missing students in need is the biggest problem; if we miss more disadvantaged groups, it feels unjust even if total help goes up slightly.
S7.notes.Q6: Personalizing the outreach makes it feel intrusive, so I don't want to be flagged too often unless there's a real reason or an annual check-in.
S7.Q8.1: I worry that if the model gets it wrong on sensitive data like disability, it could lead to labeling rather than support, creating a digital stigma instead of helping me.

S8.notes.Q3: I'm careful about sensitive data like age or gender, but financial aid is crucial for me since I struggle with costs.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm flagged, but accuracy saves lives.
S8.notes.Q5: It's okay if we miss a few more students overall as long as no group is left behind unfairly.
S8.notes.Q6: Personal emails feel less invasive than a call, but immediate feedback matters when you're struggling.
S8.notes.Q7: More personalized outreach is more effective, so I'm okay missing some students to keep it selective and meaningful.

S9.notes.Q3: Sensitive data requires higher thresholds, but some overlaps exist between my background and these categories.
S9.notes.Q4: Black boxes are unacceptable for me as a student; I need to understand why support is offered or denied.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness matters more than pure catch-all rates, especially when existing biases exist against international students like me.
S9.notes.Q6: Immediate support is better than annual checks; I don't want to miss my crisis point waiting for a yearly review.
S9.notes.Q7: Generic emails are fine for many, but personalized ones must be selective because of privacy concerns when it gets deep.
